# Executive Summary

Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in women worldwide. After biopsy, standard histological and immunohistochemical assessment typically takes one to two weeks, creating a bottleneck in treatment planning. This project develops two gene expression-based classifiers — a binary cancer versus normal classifier and a PAM50 multiclass subtype classifier — trained on publicly available GEO microarray datasets and deployed in an interactive Shiny application for clinical decision support.

The binary classifier (Elastic Net, 50-gene panel) achieved AUC 0.97, sensitivity 0.945, and specificity 0.806 on an independent external test set (GSE29044, n = 109). The multiclass classifier (Elastic Net, 130-gene panel) achieved a bootstrap mean accuracy of 88.7% on a stratified hold-out set, with per-patient 95% bootstrap CIs providing graded uncertainty estimates. Both classifiers output calibrated probability vectors with confidence bands, enabling high-confidence cases to be distinguished from borderline cases requiring additional review.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Aim and Background

## Background

Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in women worldwide, with approximately 2.3 million new cases annually (Sung et al., 2021). After a suspicious lesion is identified on mammography or ultrasound, a core needle biopsy is taken. The tissue is formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded (FFPE), then assessed histologically. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) determines oestrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and HER2 status. This process typically takes one to two weeks and requires specialist pathologist review. In resource-limited settings, or in the lead-up to weekly Multidisciplinary Team (MDT) meetings, this turnaround time creates a bottleneck in treatment planning. 

Gene expression profiling provides molecular information complementary to histological assessment. The Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) contains thousands of curated breast tissue microarray samples with matched clinical labels, collected from patients across multiple countries and institutions (Edgar et al., 2002). These datasets originate from clinical biopsy samples, where RNA was extracted from breast tissue and analysed using microarray technology to measure expression levels across thousands of genes. The resulting gene expression matrices and associated clinical annotations were subsequently deposited into GEO for public access. These datasets offer an opportunity to build data-driven classifiers that could support or accelerate pathological diagnosis.

The NanoString PanCancer 360 panel is the current clinical standard for tumour expression profiling, measuring 770 to 800 gene probes from RNA extracted directly from FFPE biopsy tissue (NanoString Technologies). Our GEO microarray datasets are generated from bulk RNA extracted from the same FFPE biopsy source material. We propose selecting the genes overlapping with the NanoString PanCancer 360 panel from our microarray data, grounding our feature selection in clinically validated gene space.Aim

## Aim

This project aims to develop two classifiers from publicly available breast tissue gene expression data: a binary classifier to distinguish malignant from normal tissue, and a PAM50 multiclass subtype classifier to assign tumours to one of five molecular subtypes (Perou et al., 2000; Parker et al., 2009). Both classifiers will be deployed in an interactive Shiny web application accessible to clinicians without programming knowledge.

The classifiers will be trained on samples (datasets collected) from multiple countries and validated on a geographically independent external test set to evaluate generalisability across populations and platforms. Predictions will be accompanied by uncertainty estimates to distinguish high-confidence results from borderline cases requiring additional review.

The tool aims to support MDT preparation, where cases can be pre-sorted by prediction confidence before the weekly meeting to facilitate more focused clinical discussion.

## Part B.1 — Binary Classifier

### B.1.1  Dataset Selection

Eight GEO datasets were collected for binary classification.\
"GSE10810", "GSE29431", "GSE42568", "GSE45827", "GSE54002", "GSE65194", and "GSE7904" were used as training datasets, while GSE29044 was reserved as an external testing dataset.

All datasets were generated on the GPL570 platform, which reduces platform heterogeneity, probe inconsistency, and gene intersection loss across studies. 

Following the preprocessing pipeline described in Part A and train-only batch correction. principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on the merged binary classification training datasets to assess cross-study integration and biological separability.

Cancer and normal samples demonstrated broad separation across the principal component space, indicating the presence of discriminative biological signal suitable for downstream classification. In contrast, samples from different datasets showed substantial overlap rather than strong dataset-specific clustering, suggesting that preprocessing and batch correction successfully reduced inter-study technical variation and dataset-specific batch effects.

### B.1.2  Label Assignment

Tumour status labels were extracted from GEO sample metadata using dataset-specific parsing rules. Samples were mapped into binary classes (“Cancer” and “Normal”) using controlled vocabulary matching and regular expression filtering applied to the original clinical annotations. For datasets containing molecular subtype annotations (e.g., GSE45827 and GSE29431), all tumour subtypes were consolidated into the “Cancer” class for binary classification. 

### B.1.3  Gene Selection

Differential expression analysis (limma) was applied to the training datasets to identify discriminative genes between cancer and normal samples.

A panel size sweep was conducted across different top-N gene sets to evaluate the trade-off between classification performance and clinically feasible assay size. Different gene panel sizes were compared based on downstream model performance.

The top 50 genes were ultimately selected, as this panel size achieved strong classification performance while maintaining a relatively low extraction and assay cost for potential clinical deployment.

### B.1.4  Model Selection

Multiple classifiers were evaluated using leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) cross-validation, including Logistic Regression, Ridge Regression, Elastic Net, Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, k-Nearest Neighbours, and Naive Bayes. Model performance was ranked using mean AUC across all validation folds. When multiple models achieved highly similar AUC values, balanced accuracy was used as a secondary ranking criterion to prioritise models with more stable performance under dataset imbalance. 

An ensemble framework was also explored using an attention-based meta-model. Base models were first evaluated according to both predictive performance (mean AUC) and pairwise prediction correlation. Three models with relatively strong performance and low inter-model correlation were selected as ensemble candidates to maximise model diversity.

Predicted probabilities from the selected base models were then used as input to an attention-based meta-model, which learned dynamic sample-specific weighting across models during prediction. The overall ensemble workflow is illustrated in Figure X.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

### B.1.5  Output

The classifier outputs a probability score P(Cancer) for each patient, with P(Normal) = 1 − P(Cancer). Patients are classified as Cancer or Normal using a fixed decision threshold of 0.5. Prediction confidence is defined as the maximum predicted class probability.

The main risk score shown for each patient is generated by the selected final model trained on the complete non-resampled training datasets.

To estimate prediction uncertainty at the patient level, an additional bootstrap procedure was performed by refitting the final model 100 times on balanced bootstrap resamples of the training data. Due to the substantial class imbalance across datasets, equal numbers of Cancer and Normal samples were sampled during each bootstrap iteration to improve prediction stability, particularly for the Normal class. These 100 bootstrap models generated 100 predicted cancer probabilities per patient, from which probability ranges and confidence bands were derived.

A separate bootstrap procedure was also applied at the dataset evaluation level. External test datasets were repeatedly resampled to estimate uncertainty for evaluation metrics, including AUC, sensitivity, precision, balanced accuracy, and F1-score. This provides uncertainty estimates for both individual patient predictions and overall model performance.

### B.1.6 External Validation

The binary classifier was evaluated on an independent external test dataset (GSE29044), which was fully withheld during model development and training. GSE29044 was selected as the external testing dataset because it provided the most balanced class distribution among the available datasets, containing 73 Cancer samples and 36 Normal samples.

## Part B.2 — Multiclass Classifier

### B.2.1  Dataset Selection

Four GEO datasets with PAM50 subtype annotations were used. Three datasets were profiled on GPL570. GSE25066 was profiled on GPL96, a platform with fewer probes, which reduces the shared gene space after intersection. Platform heterogeneity is addressed by confining gene selection to the intersecting gene set and by applying fold-internal batch correction (ComBat) within each LODO fold.

### B.2.2  Label Assignment

PAM50 subtype labels were extracted from GEO sample metadata. The Basal-like subclass includes triple-negative breast cancer, which overlaps with Basal-like tumours approximately 70–80% and are clinically treated equivalently. The five labels, Basal/TNBC, HER2, Luminal A, Luminal B, and Normal-like, were mapped from raw metadata using a controlled vocabulary with regular expression matching. Normal-like samples originate exclusively from GSE21653, meaning LODO performance metrics for this subtype are unreliable and should not be interpreted as a valid generalisation estimate.

### B.2.3  Gene Selection

OvR differential expression (limma) was applied to batch-corrected training data within each LODO fold, selecting the top N genes per contrast from the full intersecting gene set. A panel size sweep across 5 to 50 genes per class was conducted, evaluating each panel size on balanced accuracy, MCC, and high-confidence prediction percentage. High-confidence rate was included because a clinically deployed classifier must not only be accurate but also produce clinically actionable predictions. The deployed panel is determined by a single selection pass on the full batch-corrected dataset, yielding a fixed gene list independent of fold assignments. This directly informs the number of probes required for a potential NanoString assay. 

### B.2.4  Model Selection

Twenty models, including weighted variations, were evaluated. Ensembling was tested but produced no improvement at additional computational cost. Model selection prioritised mean balanced accuracy as the primary criterion, with mean MCC as a secondary tiebreaker. AUC, while it can identify good models, was excluded as a selection criterion because it saturates under clear class separation and is uninformative for identifying the best model. Balanced accuracy directly reflects per-class recall under class imbalance, and MCC accounts for all quadrants of the confusion matrix simultaneously. 

Random Forest was excluded as its non-winning class probabilities are uninformative, degrading the clinical utility of the full probability vector output. 

kNN was excluded since predicted probabilities are restricted to multiples of 1/k, rendering the probability vector clinically uninterpretable. 

### B.2.5  Output

The classifier outputs P(Basal/TNBC), P(HER2), P(Luminal A), P(Luminal B), P(Normal-like) per patient. Predicted subtype is the argmax; confidence is the maximum probability. Bootstrap CIs (B = 200 training resamples, fixed lambda) provide per-patient 95% probability ranges, defined as the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles across 200 refitted predictions. Patients are assigned high, moderate, or low confidence bands, with low-confidence cases flagged for review.

### B.2.6  External Validation

No independent external test set was available for the multiclass classifier. Evaluation was therefore limited to LODO cross-validation across the four available datasets. This represents a limitation relative to the binary classifier, which was validated on a fully withheld external dataset.

# Results

## A.1 Binary Classifier

### A.1.1 Model Performance and Selection

```{r fig3-binary-model-selection}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Figure 3. Binary classifier: (A) model selection by LODO AUC, (B) gene panel size sweep on external test set, (C) confusion matrix on external test set (GSE29044)."
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 12

# ── Load RDS ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
lodo_metric_tbl        <- readRDS(file.path(binary_results, "lodo_metric_tbl_binary.rds"))
top_gene_elastic_results <- readRDS(file.path(binary_results, "top_gene_elastic_boot_long_binary.rds"))
elastic_external_cm_df <- readRDS(file.path(binary_results, "elastic_external_cm_df_binary.rds"))
auc_tbl                <- readRDS(file.path(binary_results, "auc_tbl_binary.rds"))

# ── Panel A: Model comparison dot plot (mirrors multiclass style) ─────────────
pa_df <- lodo_metric_tbl %>%
  arrange(desc(AUC)) %>%
  mutate(
    is_best  = model == "ElasticNet",
    rank     = row_number(),
    label    = model
  )

pa <- ggplot(pa_df,
       aes(x = AUC, y = fct_reorder(label, AUC),
           colour = is_best, size = is_best)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(data = ~filter(.x, is_best),
            aes(label = sprintf("AUC = %.3f", AUC)),
            nudge_y = 0.4, fontface = "bold", size = 3.8,
            colour = "#E87722") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#E87722", "FALSE" = "grey60")) +
  scale_size_manual(values   = c("TRUE" = 5, "FALSE" = 3)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.85, 1.02)) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  labs(title = "(A) LODO Model Comparison",
       x = "LODO AUC", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

# ── Panel B: Gene sweep ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
pb_df <- top_gene_elastic_results %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(AUC, BalancedAccuracy),
               names_to = "Metric", values_to = "Value") %>%
  mutate(
    TopGenesLabel = factor(paste0("Top ", TopGenes),
                           levels = paste0("Top ", sort(unique(TopGenes)))),
    Metric = recode(Metric,
                    AUC = "AUC",
                    BalancedAccuracy = "Balanced Accuracy")
  )

# REPLACE the pb block with this:
# top_gene_elastic_results must have columns: TopGenes, Sensitivity,
# Specificity, BalancedAccuracy, AUC (one row per bootstrap iteration)

pb <- pb_df %>%
  filter(Metric == "Balanced Accuracy") %>%
  group_by(TopGenesLabel, TopGenes) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_val = mean(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_val   = sd(Value,   na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups  = "drop"
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = TopGenesLabel, y = mean_val, group = 1)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean_val - sd_val,
                  ymax = mean_val + sd_val),
              fill = "#2166AC", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2166AC", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 3.5, colour = "#2166AC") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.3f", mean_val)),
            vjust = -0.9, size = 3.2, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.4, 1.0)) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  labs(title    = "(B) Gene Panel Size Sweep — Balanced Accuracy (External Test)",
       subtitle = "Mean ± SD across 100 bootstrap resamples",
       x = "Number of top genes", y = "Balanced Accuracy") +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

# ── Panel C: Confusion matrix ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
pc <- ggplot(elastic_external_cm_df,
             aes(x = Predicted, y = Truth, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Label), size = 4.5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#F7FBFF", high = "#2C7FB8",
                      name = "Count") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")) +
  labs(title = "(C) Confusion Matrix — Elastic Net on GSE29044",
       x = "Predicted label", y = "True label")

# ── Compose figure ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(pa | pb) / pc + plot_layout(heights = c(1, 0.8))
```

Among all evaluated classifiers, Elastic Net achieved the highest overall ranking, with a mean LODO AUC of 0.9869. Based on these results, Elastic Net was selected as the final single best model for deployment in the binary risk calculator.

In addition to the final single-model selection, Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Elastic Net were selected as candidate base learners for ensemble modelling. Selection was based on a combined assessment of predictive performance and inter-model correlation. Models with strong predictive performance but lower correlation with one another were prioritised in order to maximise complementary predictive behaviour within the ensemble framework.

### External Testing Performance 

The selected single best model (Elastic Net) and the previously trained ensemble model were evaluated on the independent external testing dataset. The Elastic Net classifier achieved an AUC of 0.97, balanced accuracy of 0.88, sensitivity of 0.95, and specificity of 0.80.

The ensemble model achieved a similar AUC of 0.97, with improved balanced accuracy (0.95) and specificity (0.97), but slightly lower sensitivity (0.93). Although the ensemble model provided a modest improvement in overall balanced performance, sensitivity was prioritised due to the clinical importance of minimising missed cancer cases. In addition, the ensemble framework introduced greater complexity and reduced interpretability. Therefore, the Elastic Net model was selected as the final deployed binary classifier.

### Uncertainty Quantification

Bootstrap resampling demonstrated stable predictive performance for the final Elastic Net classifier. For the selected top-50 gene panel, the bootstrap mean AUC was 0.976 (95% CI: 0.939–0.995), while balanced accuracy remained stable at 0.876 (95% CI: 0.820–0.931). Sensitivity also remained consistently high across resampling iterations, with a bootstrap mean of 0.945 (95% CI: 0.890–0.986).

These results suggest that the classifier is robust to sampling variability and maintains stable cancer detection performance across bootstrap resamples.

## A.2 Multiclass Classifier

### A.2.1 Model Selection and Gene Panel Justification

```{r fig4-multiclass}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Figure 4. Multiclass classifier: (A) model selection by balanced accuracy, (B) gene panel size sweep justifying n=50, (C) confusion matrix on pooled LODO predictions."
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 13

# ── Load RDS ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
lodo_perf    <- readRDS(file.path(mc_results, "lodo_perf_multiclass.rds"))
ba_summary   <- readRDS(file.path(mc_results, "ba_summary_multiclass.rds"))
best_mc      <- readRDS(file.path(mc_results, "best_model_mc_multiclass.rds"))
preds_best   <- readRDS(file.path(mc_results, "preds_best_multiclass.rds"))
all_lvls     <- readRDS(file.path(mc_results, "all_lvls_multiclass.rds"))
sweep_v2     <- readRDS(file.path(mc_results, "gene_sweep_correctedv4.rds"))

# ── Panel A: Model comparison ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
mc_summary <- lodo_perf %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  summarise(
    ba_mean  = mean(mcc,       na.rm = TRUE),   # using ba from ba_summary
    mcc_mean = mean(mcc,       na.rm = TRUE),
    auc_mean = mean(macro_auc, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups  = "drop"
  ) %>%
  left_join(ba_summary %>% select(model, ba_mean), by = "model",
            suffix = c("_mcc", "")) %>%
  arrange(desc(ba_mean), desc(mcc_mean)) %>%
  mutate(
    rank    = row_number(),
    is_best = model == best_mc,
    label   = model
  )

pa_mc <- ggplot(mc_summary,
       aes(x = ba_mean, y = fct_reorder(label, ba_mean),
           colour = is_best, size = is_best)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(data = ~filter(.x, is_best),
            aes(label = sprintf("BA = %.3f", ba_mean)),
            nudge_y = 0.4, fontface = "bold", size = 3.8,
            colour = "#E87722") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.7, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#E87722", "FALSE" = "grey60")) +
  scale_size_manual(values   = c("TRUE" = 5, "FALSE" = 3)) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  labs(title = "(A) Multiclass Model Comparison (Mean Balanced Accuracy)",
       x = "Balanced Accuracy (LODO mean)", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

# ── Panel B: Gene sweep — high confidence % justifying n=50 ──────────────────
sweep_summary <- bind_rows(lapply(sweep_v2, function(r) {
  if (is.null(r)) return(NULL)
  tibble::tibble(
    n_per_class   = r$n_per_class,
    n_genes       = r$n_panel_genes,
    lodo_ba       = r$lodo_metrics$`Balanced Acc`,
    lodo_mcc      = r$lodo_metrics$MCC,
    hold_ba       = r$hold_metrics$`Balanced Acc`,   # ← add
    hold_mcc      = r$hold_metrics$MCC,              # ← add
    pct_high_conf = if (!is.null(r$risk_bands))
      round(100 * r$risk_bands["High confidence"] / sum(r$risk_bands), 1) else NA
  )
}))

# REPLACE the pb_mc pivot_longer with:
pb_mc <- sweep_summary %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(hold_ba, pct_high_conf),
               names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(
    metric = recode(metric,
      hold_ba       = "Balanced Accuracy (Hold-out)",
      pct_high_conf = "% High-confidence patients"
    ),
    value_scaled = if_else(grepl("High-confidence", metric),
                           value / 100, value)
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n_genes, y = value_scaled,
             colour = metric, group = metric)) +
  geom_line(aes(linetype = grepl("High-confidence", metric)),
            linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "dashed", "FALSE" = "solid"),
                        guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Balanced Accuracy (Hold-out)" = "#2166AC",
    "% High-confidence patients"   = "#35964F"
  )) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  labs(title    = "(B) Gene Panel Size Sweep — Hold-out Performance",
       subtitle = "Dashed = high-confidence % (÷100 for scale)",
       x = "Total unique panel genes",
       y = "Score (high-conf shown as %÷100)",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

# ── Panel C: Confusion matrix ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
display_lvls <- setdiff(all_lvls, "Normal-like")

cm_mc <- preds_best %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(truth), truth != "", truth != "Normal-like") %>%
  mutate(
    truth = factor(truth, levels = display_lvls),
    pred  = factor(pred,  levels = display_lvls)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::count(truth, pred) %>%
  tidyr::complete(truth, pred, fill = list(n = 0)) %>%
  group_by(truth) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup()

pc_mc <- ggplot(cm_mc, aes(x = pred, y = fct_rev(truth), fill = pct)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label   = if_else(n > 0, sprintf("%d\n(%.0f%%)", n, pct * 100), "0"),
        colour  = pct > 0.5),
    size = 3.5, fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours = c("#FFFFFF", "#C6DBEF", "#2166AC"),
    limits  = c(0, 1), name = "Row %"
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "black", "TRUE" = "white"),
                      guide  = "none") +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(axis.text.x  = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 0),
        panel.grid   = element_blank()) +
  labs(title    = paste0("(C) Confusion Matrix — ", best_mc, " (Pooled LODO)"),
       subtitle = "Rows = true subtype; % = row-normalised recall",
       x = "Predicted subtype", y = "True subtype")

# ── Compose ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(pa_mc | pb_mc) / pc_mc + plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.1))
```

### A.2.2 Model Performance

The top models by balanced accuracy and MCC were penalised multinomial regression models: ElasticNet, Ridge, and Lasso. ElasticNet was selected as it combines L1 sparsity with L2 stability, performing best on balanced accuracy and MCC. Non-regression approaches performed consistently worse: LDA showed competitive balanced accuracy but poor calibration, and XGBoost underperformed substantially, likely due to insufficient samples per fold for gradient boosting to converge. The stacked ensemble produced no improvement over the single best model, confirming that the additional complexity was not justified. 

### A.2.3 Lamba Optimization

Lambda was selected via 10-fold cross-validation within cv.glmnet, which selects the lambda minimising CV deviance. Alpha was fixed at 0.5 following empirical comparison of pure Lasso (alpha = 1) and Ridge (alpha = 0) as boundary cases. The number of non-zero coefficients at lambda.min confirms the model operates in a sparse regime, retaining only the most discriminative genes per subtype contrast.

### A.2.4 Gene Panel

The panel size sweep across 5 to 50 genes per class revealed that AUC plateaued rapidly across panel sizes. In contrast, balanced accuracy, MCC, and high-confidence predictions continued to improve. The final deployed model takes 207 unique genes as input, selected via one-versus-rest differential expression across five subtype contrasts. Inter-panel overlap was limited, with most subtypes sharing fewer than 20 genes, confirming largely distinct transcriptional programmes per subtype. Top-ranked genes were biologically coherent with known PAM50 biology: ERBB2 and GRB7 for HER2, ESR1 and GATA3 for the Luminal subtypes, and loss of luminal marker expression for Basal/TNBC.

### A.2.5 Per-Class Sensitivity and Specificity

Evaluated on a stratified hold-out set (n = 256), the Elastic Net model achieved a bootstrap mean accuracy of 88.7% and a median predicted confidence of 91.1%. Subtype-level performance varied: HER2 achieved the highest sensitivity (0.898), though specificity was moderate (0.687), reflecting spillover predictions into the HER2 class from mostly Basal/TNBC. Luminal A and B sensitivity were similar 0.659 with high specificity (0.943). Basal/TNBC showed perfect specificity (1.000) but sensitivity of only 0.427, attributable in part to data imbalance. Normal-like sensitivity is not reported from LODO evaluation as all samples originate from a single dataset; the deployed model is trained on these samples and capable of predicting this subtype prospectively.

### A.2.6 Uncertainty Quantification

The 91.1% median predicted confidence has a mean bootstrap 95% CI width of 24.1%, indicating moderate uncertainty in predicted subtype probabilities. Of 256 hold-out patients, 196 (77%) received a high-confidence classification, and 22 (9%) were flagged as low-confidence for clinical review. Model disagreement analysis confirmed that incorrectly classified samples cluster at lower confidence values, validating the confidence score as a clinically meaningful signal for flagging ambiguous cases.

## B. Shiny Application

![](images/clipboard-3325305555.png)

**Figure 5.** Shiny application dashboard for breast cancer risk assessment.

The Shiny application was developed to translate the trained breast cancer classification models into an interactive patient-level risk calculator (Figure 5). Users can upload gene expression datasets in CSV, TXT, or GEO txt.gz format. The application automatically identifies patient profiles, maps probe identifiers to gene symbols when required, and performs quality checks to ensure that the uploaded data contain the genes required by the prediction model.

After a patient is selected, the final Elastic Net classifier generates a risk score between 0 and 1, together with a risk category and a 95% bootstrap confidence interval to indicate prediction uncertainty. For medium- and high-risk patients, a secondary multiclass model predicts the most likely molecular subtype and displays subtype probabilities, providing additional biological interpretation.

To improve clinician usability and interpretability, the dashboard was designed as a simplified and interactive interface with seven functional components (Figure 5): (1) Input/Upload, (2) Patient Selection and Options, (3) Main Risk Summary, (4) Molecular Subtype Assessment, (5) Gene Expression Visualisation, (6) Gene Expression Summary Table, and (7) Clinical Use Notes. These modules guide users from data upload and quality assessment through prediction and interpretation.

The dashboard also includes gene-expression visualisations that compare the selected patient with reference samples, allowing potentially abnormal biomarkers to be identified. In addition, key contributing genes and summary statistics are displayed to improve model transparency and support interpretation of prediction results.

The final application was deployed through shinyapps.io, enabling interactive access across devices and allowing users to explore prediction results in real time. This deployment demonstrates how machine-learning models can be translated into a practical clinical decision-support tool.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Discussion and Conclusion

In a potential future clinical workflow, biopsy-derived gene expression profiles could be uploaded directly into the application, allowing rapid AI-assisted tumour identification, subtype prediction, and confidence estimation prior to MDT discussion and treatment planning.

# Appendix

## Appendix A — Binary Model: Feature Selection and Uncertainty

```{r appendix-binary-uncertainty}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Appendix A. Binary classifier uncertainty across gene panel sizes on GSE29044."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8

elastic_metric_summary <- tryCatch(
  readRDS(file.path(binary_results,
    "elastic_metric_summary_binary.rds")),
  error = function(e) NULL
)

if (!is.null(elastic_metric_summary)) {
  metric_labels <- c(
    AUC             = "AUC",
    Sensitivity     = "Sensitivity",
    Specificity     = "Specificity",
    BalancedAccuracy = "Balanced accuracy",
    F1              = "F1 score",
    NPV             = "NPV",
    Precision       = "Precision",
    MCC             = "MCC",
    Brier           = "Brier score"
  )

  plot_df <- elastic_metric_summary %>%
    filter(metric %in% names(metric_labels)) %>%
    mutate(
      metric_label = factor(
        unname(metric_labels[as.character(metric)]),
        levels = rev(unname(metric_labels))
      )
    )

  ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = point_estimate, y = metric_label)) +
    geom_linerange(aes(xmin = ci_lower, xmax = ci_upper),
                   linewidth = 1.1, colour = "#4C78A8") +
    geom_point(size = 2.8, colour = "#E45756") +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.05),
                       breaks = c(0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00)) +
    theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
    theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.minor   = element_blank()) +
    labs(title    = "Elastic Net Metric Uncertainty on GSE29044 — Top 50",
         subtitle = "100 class-stratified bootstrap resamples (95% percentile interval)",
         x = "Metric value", y = NULL)
} else {
  cat("elastic_metric_summary not found — run binary pipeline first.\n")
}
```

## Appendix B — Multiclass Model: Comprehensive Metrics

```{r appendix-multiclass-metrics}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Appendix B. Multiclass confusion matrix and per-class performance for all four PAM50 subtypes."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

sens_spec_tbl <- tryCatch(
  readRDS(file.path(mc_results, "sens_spec_tbl_multiclass.rds")),
  error = function(e) NULL
)

if (!is.null(sens_spec_tbl)) {
  sens_spec_tbl %>%
    filter(!is.na(sensitivity)) %>%
    pivot_longer(cols = c(sensitivity, specificity),
                 names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") %>%
    mutate(metric = tools::toTitleCase(metric)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = subtype, y = value, fill = metric)) +
    geom_col(position = "dodge", alpha = 0.85, width = 0.6) +
    geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.3f", value)),
              position = position_dodge(width = 0.6),
              vjust = -0.4, size = 3.2, fontface = "bold") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.7, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Sensitivity" = "#2166AC",
                                 "Specificity" = "#35964F")) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.1)) +
    theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
    labs(title    = "Per-class Sensitivity & Specificity — Pooled LODO (ElasticNet)",
         subtitle = "Dashed line = 0.70 reference",
         x = NULL, y = "Score", fill = NULL) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
} else {
  cat("sens_spec_tbl not found — run multiclass pipeline first.\n")
}
```
